stories.title: Robert Pether returning to Ireland after Iraqi detention
stories.summary: Robert Pether, a construction engineer, who has been held in Iraq for five years, is returning to Ireland this morning. The 51-year-old was arrested in April 2021 alongside his CME Consulting colleague, Egyptian Khalid Radwan, amid a contract dispute between the consulting firm he worked for and the Central Bank of Iraq. The bank had accused the men of stealing money from the project. After being held without charge for almost six months, and then subjected to a speedy trial, the two were each given a five-year jail sentence and fined millions of dollars. The UN had said Mr Pether's detention was illegal, and an international court had ruled his employer was not responsible for the business disagreement. A 2022 UN report determined that the case contravened international law.

stories.title: Picket line dilemma forces cancellation of Dáil sitting
stories.summary: This week's strike action by 300,000 public sector workers will also affect the work of politicians. It was confirmed yesterday that Wednesday’s Dáil sitting would be cancelled due to the one-day work stoppage. Leinster House workers are an integral part of the operations of the Dáil and Seanad. But as public sector employees, they are also party to the ongoing industrial action which is set to ratchet up on Wednesday with a full strike. This would mean picket lines at Leinster House, and opposition politicians immediately declared that they would not cross those lines. "The Government are intent on scheduling business when it seems clear at this stage that we will have national strikes, with the Houses of the Oireachtas impacted," said Labour Party whip Duncan Smith.

stories.title: Wednesday Dáil sitting cancelled over strike action
stories.summary: The Dáil will not sit next Wednesday due to the public sector strike day, in a move the opposition is describing as a climbdown by the government. Instead of the usual three-day schedule, the lower house will only meet on Tuesday and Thursday next week. Committee and Seanad business are also cancelled for Wednesday. The Government had initially pushed for the Dáil to go ahead on Wednesday with a suggestion that unions might give officials a derogation. Opposition party members had insisted they would not cross picket lines. No derogation was agreed, and government chief whip Mary Butler today tabled a revised schedule for Tuesday and Thursday of next week only.

stories.title: Is there an AI evangalist in your office? Here's what to do
stories.summary: Analysis: The gulf between AI's promise and the reality does not seem to discourage evangalists, but there are other ways to deal with this nuisance Artificial Intelligence is everywhere. Each week, we are inundated with stories telling us that AI will soon destroy civilisation, will take all of our jobs, will unleash a new era of scientific discovery, and that the bubble is about to burst, potentially taking the world economy down with it. There seems to be only one thing we can be sure of and that is nobody knows how AI will affect our lives. In your workplace, there is almost certainly an AI evangelist (maybe even more than one), people who are convinced that AI is the best thing since sliced bread and that the solution to just about any problem in organisations is "more AI". If you are lucky, they work in some other department. If you are very lucky, they are not the CEO or some high-level executive who can turn his (they are almost always men) AI obsession into marching orders for you and your co-workers. The pressure to use AI can be overwhelming, sometimes leading workers to engage in performative AI use and pretending to use AI to satisfy some order or mandate. AI evangelism can be a major source of stress. First, workers often receive orders to use more AI without any clear understanding of how to use it or what sorts of problems AI can or cannot solve. Second, AI is a potentially confusing world of models, platforms, and applications. Should you use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, xAI, Grok or something else? There is a growing suite of tools designed to help you choose among AI models or to compare the results of different models when applied to the same problem. In a sense, this just adds to the potential confusion since many AI users will not have a clear idea of which tool to use or why. There are signs that organisational pressures to use AI for everything are starting to subside. AI can be useful, but it is also potentially expensive, and it is not always a good idea to throw AI at a task that can already be done inexpensively and well by humans. Indeed, fears about an AI bubble are partially driven by reports that companies are seeing very poor returns on their investment in AI. At least so far (and probably for the foreseeable future), investments in AI have not led to notably higher productivity, innovation, or profits in most organisations. It is unlikely that the returns from applying AI to business problems in the near term will come close to the trillions that are being invested in building AI infrastructure.

stories.title: Irish man recounts 'horrific' Riyadh Airport attack
stories.summary: An Irish national, who was caught up in the attack at Riyadh Airport, said he was "lucky to be alive". He had arrived at King Khalid International Airport shortly before the missile attack occurred. The man described seeing "a large flash of light followed by the sound of a large explosion". He said while he was shielded from the worst of the blast, he saw "blood and glass everywhere". The man said "women were screaming for their children" and he said "lots of people had head injuries". The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said it is aware of a case involving an Irish national being injured in the attack and is providing consular assistance.

stories.summary: The SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race enters its final few furlongs at Tallaght Stadium tonight and a faller four out could see Shamrock Rovers or Bohemians lose the momentum to get over the line. Every game is crucial in this three-way battle – St Pat's able to sit back and watch from afar ahead of Friday’s game against Shelbourne – and defeat for Bohs in particular would surely spell the end game for their hopes of landing a first title since 2009. Alan Reynolds’ side trail Rovers by three points yet any sort of win would see them move top for four days at least. Rovers, by contrast, are well used to these high-pressure situations as they chase a sixth title in seven years. Most of those were won with relative ease, but they did have to fend off a late Derry surge last year, and manager Stephen Bradley feels that banked experience could be crucial. "What’s great about the group is we have real experience built up in understanding what it takes to go the long haul in a season," he said. "We’ve done it for so long. What comes with that is real trust and belief and understanding. Trust the process in what we do.

stories.title: Late goal denies Fenagh as Leitrm final goes to replay
stories.summary: Ballinamore secred a dramatic draw when Tom Prior fired to the Fenagh St Caillin's net in the 63rd minute at the end of an exciting Leitrim decider in Carrick on-Shannon. Ballinamore got off to a flying start with Paul Moran, Paul Honeyman and Keelan McHugh firing over a point each in the opening two minutes. Fenagh reduced the deficit to the minimum over the next five minutes after Oisin McLoughlin converted a free and Riordan O'Rourke fisted over. The Fenagh men took the lead for the first time in the game when Ryan O'Rourke converted a penalty on the 13 minute mark. But Ballinamore got back on level terms over the next seven minutes thanks to Dillon Beirne and Paul Moran who both split the Fenagh uprights. Fenagh grabbed a two point lead by the 24th minute after Fergal McLoughlin and Oisin McLoughlin slotted over a point each. Ballinamore edged ahead by the minimum as the interval approached thanks to points from Dillon Beirne, Keelan McHugh and Paul Moran (free). However a Riordan O'Rourke Fenagh point before the half-time whistle sent the sides in level at half-time, 0-08 to 1-05. After the restart Ballinamore grabbed a four point's advantage by the 36th minute with Paul Moran putting over a two-pointer free while Dillon Beirne, Brian Leyden and Niall McGovern chipped in with a point each.

stories.title: PL round-up: Hull held by Everton, Palace down Forest
stories.summary: Hull City retained their unbeaten home record since returning to the Premier League with an entertaining 2-2 draw against Everton at the MKM Stadium. The Tigers have returned to the top flight with an unexpected bang, tasting defeat for the first time in their final fixture before the international break at the hands of Newcastle. Brennan Johnson found the net in the 34th minute but was denied a first Premier League goal for the Toffees following a VAR check, leaving the sides to go in goalless at the break. The hosts wasted little time after the interval, however, as Joe Gelhardt opened the scoring in the 48th minute following an error by Ainsley Maitland-Niles. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall equalised seven minutes later, with Thierno Barry, who had squandered plenty of earlier chances, then putting the visitors ahead midway through the second period. Hull responded swiftly, though, with substitute Mohamed Belloumi pulling the home team level in the 74th minute.

stories.title: Cullen wants more from Leinster after 'disjointed' win
stories.summary: Leinster head coach Leo Cullen wasn't getting carried away by his side's 29-5 win against Cardiff at Laya Arena, insisting the province will have to get better after what he described as a "disjointed" performance. The defending URC champions marked their first game at the newly redeveloped RDS by scoring five tries to one against the Welsh side, as they held Cardiff at arm’s length to register their first win of the season, in front of a near sold out crowd of 20,035 people. At half time, it looked like Leinster were set to pull away from Corniel van Zyl’s side, leading 22-5 with a bonus-point already secure. However, a sloppy third quarter meant they spent much of the second half defending, before a late Jamie Osborne try killed things off. "Up and running" was how Cullen summed things up after the 24-point victory, but while he was pleased to pick up a first win of the season - with nine of the starting team making their first appearances of the season - he was far from delighted. "Lots of good stuff in the first half. Unfortunately, at the start of the second half we don't put on much of a show, it gets a bit disjointed.

stories.title: The Best & Worst Irish sketches on SNL over the years
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. Saturday Night Live has become an institution of television since its premiere in 1975 - and with the launch of SNL UK last year, there are now arguably even more relevant cultural touchpoints for Irish viewers. There have been many Irish guests and musical acts on the variety show over the years, most recently with CMAT appearing as the musical performer alongside Jeff Goldblum on SNL UK in September. But while some have embraced the opportunity to poke fun at themselves and their Irishness, others have produced moments that have landed rather less successfully… For all its comedic and writing talent, SNL has customarily gone for the low-hanging fruit when it comes to writing sketches for Irish guests: drinking, fighting, singing, potatoes, making fun of our accent and generally embracing every lazy stereotype you can imagine. However, Paul Mescal did his bit to level the score by taking the mick out of Americans in this 2024 sketch (which was cut for time on the day of broadcast, but later made available online.) Mescal plays a barman in an Irish pub who is astounded to learn of that rare phenomenon: an American tourist claiming Irish ancestry. Someone cast this man in a comedy, stat. This sketch was a great example of how to be funny without necessarily punching down - and in this case, it felt like SNL was laughing with us, not at us. Here, a cast that included Kate McKinnon, Cecily Strong, Aidy Bryant and actress Anya Taylor-Joy (with an impressive accent, it must be said), skewered the 'mythical Ireland' trope pushed by the likes of Celtic Woman. There are some top-notch lines here, including ‘Witness Irish culture the best way it was meant to be enjoyed… in Ohio’ and ‘If you liked Riverdance but wished they could move their arms, you’ll love us.’’ Several of the original Celtic Woman members took it in good humour, with Chloe Agnew claiming that SNL had "nailed it." stories.title: Eoin Colfer's Artemis Fowl to get Disney animated series
stories.summary: Wexford author Eoin Colfer’s bestselling Artemis Fowl books are to be adapted into a new animated television series for Disney Channel and Disney+. Colfer announced the news at New York Comic Con on Sunday during a panel celebrating the 25th anniversary of the first Artemis Fowl novel. The Irish writer will serve as an executive producer on the series alongside Ben Juwono and Colleen Evanson. "I am proud and delighted to be part of the formidable team that is putting the Artemis Fowl animation on screen," Colfer said. "Everyone is so talented and so positive that I feel certain the fairy world is in excellent hands." The fantasy adventure will follow 13-year-old genius Artemis Fowl as he discovers a hidden world of technologically advanced fairies and sets out to capture one to steal its magic and save his family.

stories.title: Read an extract of Páraic Kerrigan's 'Pop Culchie'
stories.summary:
Páraic Kerrigan's Pop Culchie: The Irish Popular Culture that Made Us is an exploration of how popular culture has shaped Irish culture and history over the last half-century. From the rise of Irish reality television and the country's first music video programme MT-USA, to forgotten chart acts, moral panics, tabloid sensations and unlikely national icons, Pop Culchie explores the stories behind the pop culture moments that defined us. Below is an extract from Chapter 2: Gas Housewives: Cookers, 'Lovely Girls' and The Calor Gas Housewife of the Year Competition. It is 1989 and on the stage of Dublin’s Olympia Theatre, Margaret Witherow, a mother of three from Convoy, Co. Donegal, stands under the bright lights beside Ireland’s beloved broadcaster Gay Byrne. As their conversation unfolds, Gay asks Margaret if she would recite a poem. Margaret, composed but a little nervous, agrees. Gay, raising an eyebrow, asks: ‘And you wrote it yourself?’ Margaret nods firmly. ‘Well done,’ Gay responds, as the room settles into a hush and Margaret begins to recite her poem, to the packed audience in the Olympia and the hundreds of thousands watching her at home on television: ‘Out of bed at seven, before I’d even yawned, a little
voice called "Mammy",
Another day had dawned.
I organised the breakfast, I was feeling none too bright,
"Mammy, have you seen my shoes, I left them here
last night."
One final check, now off you go, hurry here’s the bus,
While my easy-going husband can’t understand the fuss.
I grabbed a cup of coffee, Gaybo’s coming on,
Himself shouts from the bathroom, the sheep are on
the lawn.
I ran into the garden, still in my dressing gown,
And ran into the postman, I almost knocked him down.
He handed me a letter, another bill alas,
But no an invitation, from Calor Kosangas.
And so it was that morning, that I first got to hear,
That I had been nominated, for Housewife of the Year.’ As Margaret finishes her poem, the audience bursts into applause. Gay Byrne shakes her hand, plants a kiss on her cheek repeating, ‘Good girl, good girl’. Meanwhile, to really seal the deal, a pre-recorded segment rolls, showing Margaret’s cooking skills. She proudly presents her pièce de resistance, a leg of lamb, tastefully adorned with white heather for luck.

stories.title: More secondary school teachers begin industrial action
stories.summary: Members of the Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI) are the latest public sector workers to commence industrial action over delays in agreeing a new pay deal with the Government. They join members of the other main teaching unions, the INTO and the ASTI, who began industrial action last week. More than 23,000 TUI members in secondary schools and institutes of further and higher education will not respond to work emails or calls outside their timetabled or contracted working hours. Members in second-level schools will also withdraw from Croke Park hours. These are additional hours that teachers are required to work as part of an industrial relations agreement that came into effect in 2010. The action comes ahead of a nationwide strike on Wednesday that will see more than 300,000 public sector workers engage in a work stoppage and take to the picket lines.

stories.title: Wheelchair basketball team plans Israel match gesture
stories.summary: Members of the Irish women's wheelchair basketball team plan to bow their heads during the national anthem and wear black armbands as they face Israel in the qualifiers for the Women's B division European Championship. Their game against Israel is scheduled for Wednesday 14 October. The team will take similar action to that taken by Republic of Ireland football players during their two UEFA Nations League games against Israel. The decision to go ahead with the match has been criticised by groups including Irish Sport for Palestine and Irish Healthcare Workers for Palestine who have called on the Irish team to cancel and boycott the game. Sinn Féin Senator Chris Andrews also raised the issue in the Seanad last month, saying that the Irish Wheelchair Association (IWA) was a national charity which received significant national funding. He said at the time: "This issue should not receive less scrutiny because it is a wheelchair basketball team, rather than a football team. Disability sport should not be patronised and held to a different standard."

stories.title: Govt wants to honour RTÉ funding agreement - Taoiseach
stories.summary: The funding was expected to reach €260 million for 2027 as part of a €725m three-year agreement but instead will stand at €240m - representing a decrease of €20m. Mr O'Donovan said the decrease was due to his dissatisfaction with what he called the broadcaster's progress in implementing promised reforms. In an email to staff on Wednesday, Mr Bakhurst said that the decision "is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy". Mr Bakhurst attended a meeting with Mr O'Donovan yesterday, and he described the outcome of those talks as "extremely constructive". "I’m not going into specifics and timelines. I mean, just I can tell you, 48 hours before Budget, there was a lot of issues that I was dealing with in terms of both expenditure and on social protection. Those were the bigger issues that I was focused on in terms of specific areas around cost of disability payment." Asked whether Mr O’Donovan had gone on a "solo run", the Taoiseach said he would not characterise it in that way and he said the estimates was a tough process for everybody.

stories.title: First Home Scheme supports over 6,500 home purchases
stories.summary:
The First Home Scheme said it has supported over 6,500 home purchases to date, with over 12,000 approvals since it was established in 2022. More than a third (37%) of total First Home Scheme drawdowns have come in the past year alone. The scheme was set up to provide funding to first-time buyers who, despite having a deposit and mortgage approval in place, still could not cover the cost of a new-build home. In exchange for providing funding, the scheme takes an equity stake of up to 30% in the home. A joint venture between the State and three main banks, AIB (including EBS and Haven), Bank of Ireland and PTSB, it remains open to other authorised mortgage lenders in the Irish market.

The scheme has provided almost €440m in support to people who have bought or self-built their homes, while a total of over 27,000 potential buyers or self-builders have registered their interest in the scheme. The average purchase price for homes purchased, or construction cost for homes built, using the scheme is about €395,000 - the average support being provided by the First Home Scheme in these cases is about €67,000, or 17% of the average purchase price. 67% of First Home Scheme users are also availing of the Help to Buy scheme.

stories.title: Nepal urges villagers to evacuate after river floods
stories.summary: Nepali authorities have urged villagers to move to safer places after a flood in ⁠a river in the central part of the country swept away several houses and infrastructure, but there were no reports of any casualties. Two women and three men were out of contact, the national disaster authority said. The army said a further 49 people, including a foreigner, had been rescued. They did not give the person's nationality. A landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100 kilometres west of Kathmandu, blocked ‌the Budhi Gandaki River, leading ⁠to downstream flooding, authorities said. The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing. "We have asked villagers living along the river banks downstream to evacuate ‌and remain safe," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, the Gorkha district's most senior bureaucrat. The flood swept away about a dozen ⁠houses and two suspension bridges and damaged a hydroelectric project camp, carrying ‌some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority ⁠said.

stories.title: All eyes on Anfield as tainted City return to the fray
stories.summary: All told, there were better weeks from a Manchester City perspective to be facing their biggest rivals from the past decade. The head-spinning implications of Man City being found guilty on all 80 charges of financial wrongdoing, as well as on 34 of the 35 charges of failing to co-operate with the investigation, are still being digested by all and sundry. Given that Everton were hit with a 10-point deduction (reduced to six on appeal) for a single, solitary breach of the league's Profitability and Sustainability Rules, the consensus is naturally that Manchester City are, in the words of Father Dick Byrne, due an extra-special forfeit. It seems likely that they're set for an enormous points deduction, something akin to the number of years in Bernie Madoff's prison sentence. A number so large that even if Erling Haaland scored a hat-trick in every game for the rest of the season, they still wouldn't even finish above Spurs. Perhaps more intriguing is the question, 'what happens to the titles already won?' Roy Keane has already advised the City players who racked up medals by the boatload over the past decade and a half to toss them all in the bin. He forsook Michael Sheen's 'Cloughie' voice while delivering this line.

stories.title: Leinster mark RDS return with comfortable Cardiff win
stories.summary: It's business as usual for Leinster, as they marked the grand opening of their new and improved Laya Arena with a 29-5 win against Cardiff, to get up and running in the URC this season. After back-to-back defeats on their tour of South Africa, Leo Cullen’s side eased to their first victory of the campaign, as Sam Prendergast impressed in the five-try victory. The 23-year-old looked full of confidence in attack on his first start of the season and was at the heart of everything good in the Leinster performance, and there appears to be a real willingness in the out-half to bring the ball to the line, which is making both he and others a bigger attacking threat. As good as Prendergast looked with the ball in his hands, his performance off the tee will need to improve. The out-half appears to have changed the mechanics of his kicks to goal, approaching the ball more square-on, and it resulted in him missing his first three conversion attempts, two of which were sliced badly wide. All in all, it was a comfortable outing for the defending champions, who got minutes into their frontline internationals ahead of next week’s Investec Champions Cup opener against Clermont Auvergne. Four of their five tries came in the first half, as two for Jimmy O’Brien and one each for Hugo Keenan and Jack Conan had them 22-5 in front at the break, and while the second half dropoff will be a minor frustration for Cullen, they never looked in danger of being reeled in, as Jamie Osborne’s late converted try capped off the victory.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Elizabeth Magill's cultural picks
stories.summary: Northern Sky is an exhibition of new paintings by artist Elizabeth Magill at Dublin's Kerlin Gallery. Magill is one of the Kerlin's longest-standing artist collaborations, established when the gallery first opened in 1988. Since then, she has enjoyed a celebrated international career, exhibiting in multiple public and commercial galleries across UK, Europe and Asia. Of the paintings in Northern Sky, novelist Colm Tóibín writes: "The drama is these paintings is released and withheld. Sometimes there is wind; sometimes there is stillness. What is plain sits uneasily beside what is visionary. There is no simple meaning; instead, there is much ambiguity and strange, coiled beauty. Something might be about to happen, but that possibility is contained. It is as though the landscape is holding its breath and releasing its breath." A recent film I liked was called Blue Heron by a Canadian director called Sophy Romvari about her dysfunctional brother and how that impacted the whole family. Recently on Netflix, I watched a couple of good films: Harvest, an adaptation of a book by Jim Crace and another one called First They Killed My Father about the war in Cambodia from a child's perspective. The title of my current exhibition at the Kerlin Gallery came from a song written and performed by the late Nick Drake. I chose it because of his beautiful lyrics and voice, but also with my paintings I was trying to convey the stark luminosity you sometimes experience from skies in a northern hemisphere. My previous show was called By This River, from a Brian Eno song whereby all my painting were from his lyrics. But I’m drawn to many different types of music… too many to mention. I just finished, Chloe Iridjis' The Shadow of the Object, and I’m reading London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe, both very different books. Irdjis’ novel is nuanced and quietly powerful and Radden Keefe is fast-paced and based on a true family tragedy alongside the ever flowing river Thames and the distortions created by excessive wealth in the 80’s and 90’s London.

stories.title: Melanie Walters bids farewell to Strictly Come Dancing
stories.summary: Melanie Walters has become the second celebrity eliminated from this season of Strictly Come Dancing. The Gavin and Stacey actress, 64, had been paired with professional dancer Aljaz Skorjanec, 36. On Saturday night's episode, Walters and Skorjanec had performed a Charleston to Ooh Ahh… Just A Little Bit by Gina G, receiving a score of 17 from the judges. Judge Craig Revel Horwood said he "didn’t love" their dance while Motsi Mabuse encouraged her to "keep going". After finishing in the bottom two on the first two weeks of the competition, the judges sent the pair home. In this episode, they were sent into the dance-off against former footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and his partner Alexis Warr – who had received a score of 15 for their quickstep to I’m A Believer by The Monkees.

stories.title: Simple ways to tackle dark winter mornings
stories.summary: As darker mornings become part of the daily routine, getting out of bed can feel more difficult than ever. Shazna Khanom, head of clinical mental health at Bupa, explains that shorter days and a reduction of daylight during autumn and winter can have a significant impact on our energy levels. "The darkness doesn’t just impact people’s mood; it can also change their energy levels and make them feel slower. We often interpret this slowness as laziness and sluggishness, which can have a spiralling effect," says Khanom. If you find dark winter mornings particularly challenging, you’re certainly not alone. Here are 10 tips that could help make those mornings a little easier… "Carry on waking up early if that’s what you usually do," advises Khanom. "This regularity can help get our body into a healthy routine."

stories.title: One dead, 11 injured in fresh attack on Riyadh airport
stories.summary: One person was killed and 11 others were wounded in a fresh attack at Riyadh's international airport, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said. Yesterday, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on the airport that killed 13 ⁠people and wounded more than 300 others. An Irish national, who was caught up in the attack, said he was "lucky to be alive". Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 yesterday, causing a fire. The Saudi civil aviation authority said it was still assessing the damage. The coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport.

stories.title: Orange Order legal challenge over parade ban adjourned
stories.summary: A legal challenge to a decision by Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant to halt an Orange Order parade route along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown has been adjourned until Monday. Lawyers for the Orange Order are applying for the judicial review of the decision announced by Mr Bryant yesterday evening. Duty Judge Denise McBride said she recognised there was urgency in the case but said it was not an emergency, adding significant material was still to be obtained. "I can't fully understand why this case needs to be heard today in terms of (any) irredeemable prejudice," Judge Denise McBride said. "They (the Orange Order) had the right to walk but they couldn’t exercise it, now the right has been taken away. "In practical terms they are in exactly the same position," she added.

stories.title: Irish officials say deal reached on EU savings union
stories.summary: Irish officials say a deal has been reached between EU finance ministers on a key element of the proposed Savings and Investment Union (SIU), a set of new rules designed to enhance cross-border investing in order to boost Europe's competitiveness. Officials say it is the most significant "win" of the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU so far. Tánaiste Simon Harris has hailed the agreement as "a practical step towards a more integrated, competitive and resilient European economy". The agreement was hammered out at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg this morning, chaired by Mr Harris. Ministers accepted a compromise text on how deeper cross-border integration in financial services will be supervised at EU level. The SIU is a key element of the push to lower barriers to cross-border financial services, in order to deepen a pool of capital that can boost Europe's competitiveness and fund more scale-up champions.

stories.title: Irish AI company Tines announces 100 new jobs
stories.summary: Tines, an Irish-founded AI company, has announced the creation of 100 new jobs over the next two years. The roles will be in areas including product development, engineering, sales, customer service, marketing and operations. More than half of the new jobs will be entry-level, aimed at graduates and early-career professionals. The announcement comes ahead of the International AI Summit which takes place on Wednesday in Dublin. Co-headquartered in Dublin and Boston, Tines helps employees in companies to build software with AI and automate their workflows. Its customers include SAP, Mars, Reddit, Coinbase, Canva and Fin (formerly Intercom).

stories.title: Russian Yandex data centre shut down after drone attack
stories.summary: A drone attack damaged a Russian Yandex data centre east of the capital and disrupted operations at the facility, the technology and AI company has said. Yandex, often dubbed "Russia's Google", runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions. The attack, the third reported attack within a week, could signal the start of a new retaliatory campaign from Kyiv targeting Russia's internet infrastructure - weeks after Russia started hitting data centres in Ukraine. "As a result of a UAV attack, infrastructure at the Yandex data centre in Vladimir was damaged," the company said in a service alert on Telegram. No one was injured in the attack, Yandex said, adding that emergency services were at the site and the company was evaluating ways to restore operations. "Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended," it added, advising users to activate disaster-recovery plans as the platform operated in emergency mode.

stories.title: NFL: Patriots and Packers bag big wins, Jags beat Eagles
stories.summary: New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye threw for 374 yards and four touchdowns, with no interceptions, as they defeated the Las Vegas Raiders 45-17 in Foxborough. The reigning AFC champions made light work of their conference rivals to improve to 3-2, having defeated the Buffalo Bills last Sunday. Earlier, Jacksonville Jaguars kicker Cam Little landed a last-gasp 57-yard field goal to snatch his side a 19-17 win against Philadelphia Eagles in London. The Eagles appeared set to grab victory themselves when their kicker, Jake Elliott, was successful from 48 yards to edge his side 17-16 ahead with eight seconds remaining at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. But Jaguars running back Ameer Abdullah returned Elliott's kick-off all the way to the 40-yard line with just one second left and Little kept his nerve to send over his match-winning kick with the final play of the game. Minnesota Vikings extended their winning start to the NFL season to five matches as they won 23-13 at New Orleans Saints thanks to some superb defence.
